extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military officers, government lawyers, and legal scholars working on the laws of war and martial law
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes legal standards, precedents, and operative rules governing intervention, prisoners of war, parole, flags of truce, suspension of habeas corpus, and martial law as expressed in official opinions and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive duty of intervention under treaty (Cuba, art. 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervention duty accrues if an insurrectionary movement arises on Cuba and the Cuban Government is powerless or admits it has exhausted its powers, making intervention necessary to establish and maintain public order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First steps are political and advisory (notification, negotiations, good offices, compromise, redress). If pacific methods fail, issue a proclamation calling insurgents to disperse by a specific date; thereafter employ land and naval forces to restore order and remove opposition to law execution. (C. 20396, Sept. 15, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence and prerequisites for forcible intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Before use of force, the Executive should attempt political/advisory measures and a proclamation; forcible measures follow only if pacific remedies fail and proclamation conditions exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proclamation calls upon persons composing insurrectionary combinations to disperse and retire peaceably within a specific date; upon issuance, the President may employ forces to restore order. The existence of forcible uprising under treaty provisions brings the matter within Congressional authority to call forth militia. (C. 20396, Sept. 15, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to employ land and naval forces for protection of independence and order
rubrics_metrics.description: Land and naval forces may be employed under statutory authority (e.g., section 5298, R.S.) to preserve independence and secure a government adequate to protect life, property, and liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases/advisories (C. HH8, Dec. 28, 1911; 20396, Sept. 15, 1906) support use of forces when necessary to maintain public order and protect rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of retaliation by military commanders
rubrics_metrics.description: Retaliatory acts (e.g., arresting and holding an equal number of citizens until offenders are surrendered) can be warranted by the laws and usages of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two soldiers seized and delivered to enemy; commanding general ordered arrest of equal number of citizens to hold until offenders surrendered — held warranted. (R. 9, 210, June, 1864.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of flag of truce protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission under a flag of truce does not entitle persons to immunity from subsequent inquiry, restraint, or detention on reasonable grounds of suspicion; a flag of truce is not a safe-conduct beyond its immediate mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag affords merely temporary protection not to be continued after mission accomplished. Persons entering under false pretenses remain liable to arrest, trial, and punishment for violations of laws of war. (R.5,193; R.19,673; see Lieber's Instructions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlawful killing of prisoner of war constitutes murder
rubrics_metrics.description: The taking of the life of a prisoner of war, when not justified by escape, violence, or breach of discipline, is murder as fully as homicide in peacetime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: R. 7, 360, Mar., 1864. Common-law definitions and distinctions between murder and manslaughter noted; killing a confined prisoner after hostilities has ceased is murder. (State v. Gut; authorities cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation of parole punishable severely (including death)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation of parole by a paroled prisoner of war is an offense against the common law of war and is punishable with death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: R.6,20, Jan., 1864. Parole obligations under law of war are strict and violations considered grave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of civil employees serving with enemy forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil employees of the enemy serving with its army in the field are to be regarded on the same footing as soldiers and may be properly detained as prisoners of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an engineer captured while serving on an enemy steamer held as prisoner of war. (R.6,542, Aug., 1866.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of criminal acts by prisoners of war
rubrics_metrics.description: When a POW kills another prisoner or commits other criminal acts, the government may, in its discretion, turn him over for trial to State authorities, exchange him under the cartel, or leave him to be tried by enemy authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: POW who killed a fellow prisoner at a camp in a State with functioning civil courts — government might transfer him for State trial or exchange him. (R. 13, 498, Mar., 1865.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of persons of doubtful belligerent status
rubrics_metrics.description: Where serious doubt exists as to whether captured persons are legitimate belligerents (soldiers) or criminals (e.g., partisans/raiders), their status should be investigated and may be left to the civil court that assumed jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If represented as Confederate soldiers but status doubtful, advised that they be left to the court which had assumed jurisdiction so defenses of legitimate acts of war can be properly investigated. (R.2,591; R.5,344.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on parole: returning within lines/home without authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A parole conditioned on returning to one's home does not authorize a paroled enemy to come within our lines or into certain States without special authority from the United States Government; doing so may be a violation of parole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: soldiers released on parole on condition of returning to homes were held not authorized to enter Maryland without special authority; persons harboring them could be charged under article 45. (R.12,400, May, 1865.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercy/mitigation for non-hostile motives entering enemy lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an enemy comes within our lines for an innocent non-hostile purpose (e.g., to purchase Bibles), though in violation of the law of war, punishment may be remitted upon taking oath of allegiance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Confederate chaplain convicted for entering lines to purchase Bibles — advised that punishment might be remitted on taking oath of allegiance. (R.11,558, Mar., 1865.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of enlisting while a prisoner of war
rubrics_metrics.description: A prisoner of war who enlists in the enemy's service terminates his status as a prisoner of war and, generally, cannot be returned to his original army upon discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held: enlisting terminates POW status. Cited decisions: O.16, July 13, 1894; 1193, Apr. 13, 1895.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of officers/soldiers dismissed while prisoners
rubrics_metrics.description: If an officer or soldier is tried or awaiting sentence and taken prisoner before official communication of dismissal or sentence, upon exchange and return he is entitled to be treated and paid as having been in U.S. service up to the date of notification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to officers dismissed by order or soldiers dishonorably discharged by sentence under similar circumstances. (R.12,230; R.13,589; C.2039, Feb., 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Paroled prisoner remains subject to military control
rubrics_metrics.description: A paroled prisoner is a soldier placed under a disability to engage in active operations against the enemy but remains part of the Army and as much subject to military control as before capture; absence without authority may be absence without leave or desertion depending on intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C.1746, Sept., 1895; C.17937, May 4, 1905. Parole imposes restrictions but does not sever military status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paroled prisoner not necessarily bound to original command
rubrics_metrics.description: A paroled prisoner is not necessarily required to return to the regiment or command to which attached upon capture; in absence of special orders he need only abide by existing orders regarding paroled prisoners generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.39,339, Dec., 1877. Treatment depends on orders given by competent authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable duties for paroled prisoners absent contrary cartel stipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of any stipulation to the contrary in the cartel of exchange, a paroled prisoner may legally be put on duty as a post guard at a post not in the field or threatened by the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.21,592, Aug., 1866 — cartel terms control restrictions on duties while on parole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlistment under extreme duress may excuse desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Although generally a POW is justified in enlisting in the enemy's service only by a well-founded apprehension of immediate death, enlistment induced solely by extreme privation and suffering that imperils life may be excused and soldiers in that situation should not, as a general rule, be treated as deserters when returned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Federal soldiers who enlisted while prisoners under desperate conditions to escape death advised generally not to be treated as deserters and to be returned to duty without punishment; but voluntary enlistment and fighting for enemy when escape was possible may merit desertion charges. (R.11,135; R.16,136.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to suspend the writ of habeas corpus
rubrics_metrics.description: During rebellion, Congress (act of Mar. 3, 1863) authorized the President to suspend the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus whenever, in his judgment, public safety requires it. There was debate whether the President could exercise the power independently of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presidential proclamations (May 10, 1861; Sept. 24, 1862; Sept. 15, 1863) suspended the writ in various contexts; judicial authority tended to view suspension as a Congressional power. See Ex parte Merryman and other cases; opinions of Attorney General cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of presidential suspension on courts
rubrics_metrics.description: When persons are detained 'under the authority of the President' pursuant to suspension proclamations, judges and courts (state or federal) are required to dismiss writs of habeas corpus upon being so advised in the prescribed manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.15,157, May, 1865. The act of Mar.3,1863 prescribes manner of advice; courts must defer to properly executed military detentions under proclamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation of suspension does not necessarily free military detainees
rubrics_metrics.description: A presidential revocation of a general suspension of the writ (e.g., Dec. 1, 1865) does not operate to authorize a State court to discharge a prisoner detained in military custody under color of United States authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.21,92, Dec., 1865 — limits the effect of revocation on existing military detentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and nature of martial law
rubrics_metrics.description: Martial law is military authority exercised according to the rules and usages of war; 'martial law at home' is military power exercised in time of war, insurrection, or rebellion in parts of the country retaining allegiance, over persons and things not ordinarily subject to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martial law presupposes civil courts unable to enforce processes and is justified by necessity to protect society; those administering it must act in accordance with principles of justice, honor, humanity, and the laws/usages of war. It is a suspension of ordinary law replaced by military command judgment and usages. (C.8383, May, 1900; Manual for Courts-Martial.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Martial law overrides civil law but with substantive limits
rubrics_metrics.description: While martial law supersedes civil law for its duration, it does not authorize general military license; it cannot be used to justify unnecessary violence, personal persecution, or wanton wrong and must be exercised according to justice, honor, humanity and laws/usages of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subordinates may not avail themselves of martial law to commit abuses; specific precedents cited (R.12,105; R.19,41; C.8383) emphasize limits on summary/arbitrary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commencement and cessation of martial law
rubrics_metrics.description: Martial law exists when resistance to law reaches such a stage that civil authorities are powerless; it ceases when necessity ends and civil authorities can resume unobstructed functions, even if military remains present to aid them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proclamation of 'state of insurrection and rebellion' effectively declares martial law for the region, but proclamation is not essential; the condition is factual. Examples: Maryland/Baltimore orders ceased once exigency passed. (C.8383; R.12,422; R.10,669.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers of military commanders under martial law
rubrics_metrics.description: When a city or district is put under martial law by a commanding general, he becomes its supreme governor and is ordinarily presumed empowered to exercise the same authority the President might have exercised by proclamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.10,669, Dec., 1864; commander may take measures necessary to suppress resistance and restore civil authority; however, exercise must conform to principles described above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint of civil prosecutions during martial law for military necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: A military commander may, if necessary for effective maintenance of martial law and accomplishment of its ends, restrain prosecution of suits instituted against United States officers for acts done in line of duty when such prosecutions impede military operations or embarrass constituted authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.10,669, Dec., 1864 — commander discretion to restrain prosecutions that would impede military operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military forces aiding State authorities remain under federal command
rubrics_metrics.description: When the United States protects a State against 'domestic violence,' its military forces act in aid of State authorities to the extent necessary to reestablish civil authority but remain under command of military officers under the President, not under State command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.8383, May, 1900 — forces are independent in command relationship and operate under Presidential orders to perform constitutional duties toward the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who determines termination of war
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary will not, originally, be empowered to determine whether a war has terminated; courts should await and abide by action of the President or Congress on such a question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.18,293, Oct., 1865 — courts defer to the political branches on the termination status of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of termination of international war by treaty ratification
rubrics_metrics.description: A war between nations may be held to terminate on the date of exchange of ratifications of the treaty of peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Status of war between Spain and United States terminated on exchange of ratifications of peace treaty. (Multiple opinions cited: C.12888; C.12881; C.15154; etc.)
